propositions.text: The EU AI Act applies a risk-based framework with four tiers plus a parallel regime for general-purpose AI models.

The first tier covers prohibited practices: Article 5 lists eight categories of AI practice that are banned outright, including subliminal or manipulative techniques causing significant harm, exploitation of vulnerabilities, social scoring, real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement outside narrow exceptions, and others.

The second tier covers high-risk systems, which are classified on two cumulative routes under Article 6: a system is high-risk where it is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I and that product must undergo third-party conformity assessment, or where the system falls within one of the use-case categories listed in Annex III, which covers areas such as biometrics, critical infrastructure, education and vocational training, employment and worker management, access to essential private and public services, law enforcement, migration and asylum, and administration of justice.

The third tier, limited risk, applies to systems that interact directly with natural persons or generate synthetic content, which carry the transparency obligations in Article 50 without being classified as high-risk.
The fourth tier, minimal risk, covers all remaining systems and carries no mandatory obligations under the Regulation.

Running in parallel to these four tiers, general-purpose AI models are governed separately under Articles 51 to 56: Article 51 classifies a model as having systemic risk where it has high-impact capabilities, presumed when cumulative training compute exceeds 10^25 floating-point operations, or where the Commission so designates it, and Article 55 imposes additional obligations on providers of such models on top of the baseline duties in Article 53.

propositions.text: The EU AI Act applies a risk-based framework with four tiers plus a parallel regime for general-purpose AI models.

The first tier covers prohibited practices: Article 5 lists eight categories of AI practice that are banned outright, including subliminal or manipulative techniques causing significant harm, exploitation of vulnerabilities, social scoring, real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement outside narrow exceptions, and others.

The second tier covers high-risk systems, which are classified on two cumulative routes under Article 6: a system is high-risk where it is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I and that product must undergo third-party conformity assessment, or where the system falls within one of the use-case categories listed in Annex III, which covers areas such as biometrics, critical infrastructure, education and vocational training, employment and worker management, access to essential private and public services, law enforcement, migration and asylum, and administration of justice.

The third tier, limited risk, applies to systems that interact directly with natural persons or generate synthetic content, which carry the transparency obligations in Article 50 without being classified as high-risk.
The fourth tier, minimal risk, covers all remaining systems and carries no mandatory obligations under the Regulation.

Running in parallel to these four tiers, general-purpose AI models are governed separately under Articles 51 to 56: Article 51 classifies a model as having systemic risk where it has high-impact capabilities, presumed when cumulative training compute exceeds 10^25 floating-point operations, or where the Commission so designates it, and Article 55 imposes additional obligations on providers of such models on top of the baseline duties in Article 53.
